quests.instruction: Which two changes are heard in “Morning, I’ll have a hot milk and one pastry”?
quests.word: Morning, I’ll have a hot milk and one pastry
quests.textToSpeak: Morning, I’ll have a hot milk and one pastry
options: The /t/ of “hot” is omitted before “milk”, and the /n/ of “one” is omitted too
The /m/ of “milk” shifts to /t/, and the /p/ of “pastry” shifts to /n/
The /t/ of “hot” blends into /tʃ/, and the /n/ of “one” shifts to /ŋ/
“hot” shifts toward /p/ before “milk”, and “one” shifts to /m/ before “pastry”
quests.correctAnswer: “hot” shifts toward /p/ before “milk”, and “one” shifts to /m/ before “pastry”
quests.hint: Look for a tongue-tip sound before a lip sound at each of the two boundaries.
quests.explanation: “Hot” ends in /t/ before the lip sound /m/, so the /t/ can shift to the lips: “hop milk”. “One” ends in /n/ before the lip sound /p/, so the /n/ can shift to [m]: “wum pastry”. Both are place assimilation, and both occur in an ordinary café order.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar /t/ and /n/ assimilate to the bilabial place before /m/ and /p/, so one order can contain two assimilations.
quests.spokenForm: Morning, I’ll have a hop milk and wum pastry

quests.instruction: Which sound shifts in “Cheers, can I get a good cappuccino, please?”
quests.word: Cheers, can I get a good cappuccino, please
quests.textToSpeak: Cheers, can I get a good cappuccino, please
options: The /d/ of “good”, which shifts toward /g/ before the /k/
The /g/ of “good”, which shifts to /d/ before the /k/
The /k/ of “cappuccino”, which shifts to /t/ before the vowel
The /d/ of “good”, which shifts to /b/ before the /k/
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ of “good”, which shifts toward /g/ before the /k/
quests.hint: Find the tongue-tip consonant that sits right before a back-of-the-mouth sound.
quests.explanation: “Good” ends in /d/, and “cappuccino” begins with /k/, a back-of-the-mouth sound, so the /d/ can shift to [g]: “goog cappuccino”. The /k/ is the trigger and does not change. The same pattern appears in “good coffee” and similar orders.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final /d/ before a velar /k/ commonly assimilates to velar [g] in casual speech.
quests.spokenForm: Cheers, can I get a goog cappuccino, please

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Yeah, I’ll take that bun and a plain bagel”?
quests.word: Yeah, I’ll take that bun and a plain bagel
quests.textToSpeak: Yeah, I’ll take that bun and a plain bagel
options: “that bun” and “plain bagel”, with every consonant unchanged
“thap bun” and “plaim bagel”: the /t/ and /n/ shift to the lips
“thak bun” and “plaing bagel”: both shift toward the back of the mouth
“tha bun” and “pla bagel”: the /t/ and the /n/ are omitted
quests.correctAnswer: “thap bun” and “plaim bagel”: the /t/ and /n/ shift to the lips
quests.hint: Both “bun” and “bagel” begin with a lip sound. Predict what that does to the consonant before each one.
quests.explanation: “That” ends in /t/ before /b/, so the /t/ can shift to [p]: “thap bun”. “Plain” ends in /n/ before /b/, so the /n/ can shift to [m]: “plaim bagel”. A clear /t/ and /n/ are also acceptable, especially in careful speech. Hearing both changes helps you catch a quick order.
quests.phoneticRule: The same bilabial trigger /b/ pulls both /t/ and /n/ to the lips, so a short order can show two parallel assimilations.
quests.spokenForm: Yeah, I’ll take thap bun and a plaim bagel

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “seat you” fits “Evening, shall we seat you by the window?”
quests.word: Evening, shall we seat you by the window
quests.textToSpeak: Evening, shall we seat you by the window
options: “seat-you”: both sounds are separate, with a clear /j/
“sea-jew”: they blend into /dʒ/ instead
“sea-you”: the /t/ is dropped before the /j/
“sea-chew”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
quests.correctAnswer: “sea-chew”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
quests.hint: Say “seat you” quickly and listen to how the /t/ and the “y” sound combine.
quests.explanation: “Seat” ends in /t/ and “you” begins with /j/, so the pair blends into /tʃ/: “sea-chew”. Restaurant staff say this line many times a day, so the blend is very likely. Hearing it helps you understand what is being offered.
quests.phoneticRule: Offers with a verb ending in /t/ followed by “you” show the /t/ + /j/ blend at normal speed.
quests.spokenForm: Evening, shall we sea-chew by the window

quests.instruction: Which sound results where “has” and “your” meet in “Great, has your friend arrived yet?”
quests.word: Great, has your friend arrived yet
quests.textToSpeak: Great, has your friend arrived yet
options: A /ʃ/ blend: /z/ + /j/ becomes “sh”
A /ʒ/ blend: /z/ + /j/ becomes the “zh” of “vision”
A /dʒ/ blend: /z/ + /j/ becomes “j”
No blend, because “has” is stressed and keeps its /z/
quests.correctAnswer: A /ʒ/ blend: /z/ + /j/ becomes the “zh” of “vision”
quests.hint: The /z/ is voiced. Choose the blend that keeps the voicing.
quests.explanation: “Has” ends in /z/, and “your” begins with /j/, so the pair blends into /ʒ/: “ha-zhyer”. The voiced /z/ gives a voiced /ʒ/. At a restaurant door a host often asks this kind of question, so the blend is a good one to recognise.
quests.phoneticRule: A voiced /z/ before a weak “your” gives the voiced fricative /ʒ/, even in a question about a person who has arrived.
quests.spokenForm: Great, ha-zhyer friend arrived yet

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “reserved your” fits “Sure, we’ve reserved your usual table by the window”?
quests.word: Sure, we’ve reserved your usual table by the window
quests.textToSpeak: Sure, we’ve reserved your usual table by the window
options: “reserv-jyer”: the /d/ and a weak “your” blend into /dʒ/
“reserved-your”: both words strong, with a clear /j/
“reserv-chyer”: they blend into /tʃ/
“reserv-yer”: the /d/ is dropped before “your”
quests.correctAnswer: “reserv-jyer”: the /d/ and a weak “your” blend into /dʒ/
quests.hint: Say “reserved your” as a host would, and listen for a “j” sound at the join.
quests.explanation: “Reserved” ends in /d/ after a /v/ sound, and “your” begins with /j/, so the pair blends into /dʒ/: “reserv-jyer”. Past-tense endings take part in the blends. A host who has kept your table says this quickly and warmly.
quests.phoneticRule: A past-tense /d/ ending blends with a following weak “your” into /dʒ/, as in other /d/ + /j/ sequences.
quests.spokenForm: Sure, we’ve reserv-jyer usual table by the window

quests.instruction: Which /t/ is likely omitted in “Hey, I bought this last week but it’s the wrong size”?
quests.word: Hey, I bought this last week but it’s the wrong size
quests.textToSpeak: Hey, I bought this last week but it’s the wrong size
options: The /s/ of “this”, before the /l/ of “last”
The /t/ of “last”, before the /w/ of “week”
The /t/ of “but”, before the vowel of “it’s”
The /k/ of “week”, before “but”
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ of “last”, before the /w/ of “week”
quests.hint: Look for a /t/ after /s/ that is followed by a consonant.
quests.explanation: “Last” ends in /st/ before /w/, so the /t/ is often omitted: “las’ week”. The /t/ of “but” is followed by a vowel and links: “bu-tit’s”. A customer explaining a return uses these everyday phrases, so the omitted /t/ is a good one to recognise.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision of /t/ after /s/ before a consonant occurs in everyday return explanations as in any other speech.
quests.spokenForm: Hey, I bought this las’ week but it’s the wrong size

quests.instruction: Which /t/ is likely omitted in “Brilliant, we just need to check the stock first”?
quests.word: Brilliant, we just need to check the stock first
quests.textToSpeak: Brilliant, we just need to check the stock first
options: The /t/ of “first”, at the end of the sentence
The /k/ of “check”, before “the”
The /t/ of “just”, before the /n/ of “need”
The /t/ of “to”, before “check”
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ of “just”, before the /n/ of “need”
quests.hint: Look for the /t/ that is squeezed between an /s/ and the /n/ of the next word.
quests.explanation: “Just” ends in /st/ before “need”, which begins with /n/, so the /t/ is often omitted: “jus’ need”. “First” ends the sentence, so nothing follows it. Shop assistants use this phrase constantly, so the omission is typical in service talk.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final /t/ after /s/ is omitted before a following consonant in service phrases such as “just need to…”.
quests.spokenForm: Brilliant, we jus’ need to check the stock first

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Seriously, the zip broke after just one wash”?
quests.word: Seriously, the zip broke after just one wash
quests.textToSpeak: Seriously, the zip broke after just one wash
options: “jus’ one wash”: the /t/ is omitted, and “broke after” links as “bro-kafter”
“just one wash” with the /t/ released, and “broke after” separated by a clear pause between them
“jus-twun wash”: the /t/ moves onto “one”
“jus’ one wash” but “broke after” also loses its /k/
quests.correctAnswer: “jus’ one wash”: the /t/ is omitted, and “broke after” links as “bro-kafter”
quests.hint: Check each boundary: a /t/ before a consonant, and a consonant before a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Just” ends in /st/ before /w/, so the /t/ is often omitted: “jus’ one”. “Broke” ends in /k/ before the vowel of “after”, so the /k/ links: “bro-kafter”. Elision and linking therefore occur in the same complaint.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision before a consonant and linking before a vowel co-occur within a single customer complaint.
quests.spokenForm: Seriously, the zip bro-kafter jus’ one wash

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “ask him” fits “Maybe you could ask him about the test results”?
quests.word: Maybe you could ask him about the test results
quests.textToSpeak: Maybe you could ask him about the test results
options: “ask-him”: both words strong, with a clear /h/ and a break between them
“as-chim”: the /k/ and /h/ blend into /tʃ/
“as-kim”: the /h/ is dropped and the /k/ links onto the weak “him”
“as-im”: the /k/ is dropped as well as the /h/
quests.correctAnswer: “as-kim”: the /h/ is dropped and the /k/ links onto the weak “him”
quests.hint: Look at the pronoun after “ask” and decide how strong it is.
quests.explanation: “Him” is unstressed after “ask”, so it loses its /h/, and the /k/ links onto it: “as-kim”. The result is easy to mishear as “as-kim”, as if “kim” were a name. Patients and receptionists use this construction constantly.
quests.phoneticRule: An unstressed object pronoun drops /h/ after a consonant-final verb, and the consonant links onto the remaining vowel.
quests.spokenForm: Maybe you could as-kim about the test results

quests.instruction: Which /h/ sounds are most likely dropped in “Hmm, has he had his results back yet?”
quests.word: Hmm, has he had his results back yet
quests.textToSpeak: Hmm, has he had his results back yet
options: “has” only, because it begins the question
None: /h/ is kept in every position in this question, even in unstressed words
“he”, “had” and “his”: unstressed words that follow another word
All four, including “has” at the start
quests.correctAnswer: “he”, “had” and “his”: unstressed words that follow another word
quests.hint: Decide which /h/-initial word opens the question, and which ones are unstressed in the middle.
quests.explanation: “Has” begins the question and keeps its /h/. “He”, “had” and “his” follow other words and are unstressed, so they lose their /h/: “ee əd iz”. The question therefore sounds like “has ee əd iz results back yet”. Three dropped /h/ sounds in a row are common in medical talk.
quests.phoneticRule: In a run of /h/-initial function words, the first word keeps its /h/ at the start of an utterance and the unstressed ones that follow drop theirs.
quests.spokenForm: Hmm, has ee əd iz results back yet

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Listen, tell her the doctor wants to see him tomorrow”?
quests.word: Listen, tell her the doctor wants to see him tomorrow
quests.textToSpeak: Listen, tell her the doctor wants to see him tomorrow
options: Clear /h/ sounds in both pronouns, with no links
A dropped /h/ in “her” only, and a clear /h/ in “him”
A /tʃ/ blend in “tell her” and a /w/ glide before “him”, with clear /h/ sounds kept
A dropped /h/ in “her” and “him”, with a link after “tell” and a /j/ glide before “him”
quests.correctAnswer: A dropped /h/ in “her” and “him”, with a link after “tell” and a /j/ glide before “him”
quests.hint: Find the two pronouns and decide what precedes each.
quests.explanation: “Her” follows “tell” and loses its /h/, so the /l/ links onto it: “te-lər”. “Him” follows “see”, which ends in a vowel, so after the /h/ drops a /j/ glide links them: “see-yim”. Two different linking patterns come from the same /h/ dropping.
quests.phoneticRule: Dropped /h/ produces consonant-to-vowel linking after a consonant and glide linking after a vowel.
quests.spokenForm: Listen, te-lər the doctor wants to see-yim tomorrow

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Gran says she’ll make her famous stew on Sunday”?
quests.word: Gran says she’ll make her famous stew on Sunday
quests.textToSpeak: Gran says she’ll make her famous stew on Sunday
options: “she will”: two full syllables and a clear /h/ in “her”
“she’d”: the /l/ becomes a /d/
“she’ll”: one syllable, /ʃiːl/, and “her” is weak: /ə/
“shell”: a different word with a short vowel
quests.correctAnswer: “she’ll”: one syllable, /ʃiːl/, and “her” is weak: /ə/
quests.hint: Count the syllables in “she’ll” and listen to how strong “her” is.
quests.explanation: “She’ll” is a contraction of “she will”: one syllable, /ʃiːl/. “Her” is unstressed and loses its /h/: /ə/. The stressed words are “make”, “famous” and “stew”. A family plan sounds quicker than it looks on paper.
quests.phoneticRule: A contracted “’ll” is one syllable, and a following unstressed possessive “her” is weak, with its /h/ often lost.
quests.spokenForm: Gran says she’ll make er famous stew on Sunday

quests.instruction: Which contractions are heard in “Auntie says they’re going to be late so we’ll start without them”?
quests.word: Auntie says they’re going to be late so we’ll start without them
quests.textToSpeak: Auntie says they’re going to be late so we’ll start without them
options: “they’re” and “we’ll”: both are one syllable
“they’re” only; “we’ll” is two full words, “we will”
“we’ll” only; “they’re” is two full words, “they are”
Neither: contractions are not used in family talk at all
quests.correctAnswer: “they’re” and “we’ll”: both are one syllable
quests.hint: Find the two pronoun + auxiliary pairs in the sentence.
quests.explanation: “They’re” is a contraction of “they are”: /ðeə/ or /ðə/. “We’ll” is a contraction of “we will”: /wiːl/. Both are one syllable. Family plans are casual, so these contractions are the norm. “Them” is also weak: /əm/.
quests.phoneticRule: Contractions of pronoun + auxiliary are the default in casual family talk, each compressing two words into one syllable.
quests.spokenForm: Auntie says they’re gonna be late so we’ll start without ’em

quests.instruction: Which meanings do the two “’d” forms have in “Uncle says he’d’ve picked us up if he’d known”?
quests.word: Uncle says he’d’ve picked us up if he’d known
quests.textToSpeak: Uncle says he’d’ve picked us up if he’d known
options: Both stand for “would”, because both follow “he”
Both stand for “had”, because both follow “he”
The first stands for “would” (in “would have”); the second for “had” (before “known”)
The first stands for “had” (before “picked”), and the second for “would” (before “known”)
quests.correctAnswer: The first stands for “would” (in “would have”); the second for “had” (before “known”)
quests.hint: Look at the verb form that follows each “’d”.
quests.explanation: In “he’d’ve picked”, the contraction is “he would have” (the counterfactual). In “if he’d known”, “’d” stands for “had”, because “known” is a past participle. The two /d/ sounds are identical, so grammar decides each meaning.
quests.phoneticRule: Contracted /d/ is “would” when part of “’d’ve” and “had” before a past participle, so grammar disambiguates identical sounds.
quests.spokenForm: Uncle says heed-əv picked us up if heed known

quests.instruction: Which words are weak in “Hey, what are you up to on Saturday?”
quests.word: Hey, what are you up to on Saturday
quests.textToSpeak: Hey, what are you up to on Saturday
options: “what”, “up” and “Saturday”: the content words
“are”, “you”, “to” and “on”: the function words
Only “are” and “you”, because they are short
All equally strong when talking to friends
quests.correctAnswer: “are”, “you”, “to” and “on”: the function words
quests.hint: Tap the beats of the question, and listen to the quiet words between the taps.
quests.explanation: The stressed words are “what”, “up” and “Saturday”. The small words “are”, “you”, “to” and “on” are weak: /ə/, /jə/, /tə/ and /ən/. Friends say this quickly, so it can sound like “wot-uh-yuh-up-tuh-on Saturday”.
quests.phoneticRule: In an informal question about plans, the content words carry the beats and the auxiliary, pronoun and prepositions are weak.
quests.spokenForm: Hey, wot uh yuh up tuh on Saturday

quests.instruction: Which description fits “meet at” and “past six” in “Cool, shall we meet at the café at half past six?”
quests.word: Cool, shall we meet at the café at half past six
quests.textToSpeak: Cool, shall we meet at the café at half past six
options: “meet at” is separated, and “past six” keeps a clear /t/ released before the /s/
“meet at” links, but “past six” links the /t/ onto “six”
“meet at” links as “mee-tat”; “past six” loses its /t/: “pas’ six”
“meet at” loses its /t/, and “past six” is unchanged
quests.correctAnswer: “meet at” links as “mee-tat”; “past six” loses its /t/: “pas’ six”
quests.hint: Check what follows each /t/: a vowel in one place, a consonant in the other.
quests.explanation: “Meet” ends in /t/ before the vowel of “at”, so the /t/ links. “Past” ends in /st/ before /s/, so the /t/ is often omitted. Arranging a time is full of such phrases: the same /t/ sound is kept in one and dropped in the other.
quests.phoneticRule: The same /t/ is linked before a vowel and omitted before a following consonant, so one arrangement can show both.
quests.spokenForm: Cool, shall we mee-tat the café at half pas’ six

quests.instruction: Which words are weak in “Maybe we could go to the cinema and then get something to eat”?
quests.word: Maybe we could go to the cinema and then get something to eat
quests.textToSpeak: Maybe we could go to the cinema and then get something to eat
options: “go”, “cinema”, “get” and “eat”: the content words
Only “to” and “and”, because they are prepositions and conjunctions
None: plans are said word by word
“we”, “could”, “to”, “the”, “and” and “to”
quests.correctAnswer: “we”, “could”, “to”, “the”, “and” and “to”
quests.hint: Say the plan aloud and notice which words you could drop from a text message.
quests.explanation: The plan is “go… cinema… get… something… eat”. The words “we”, “could”, “to”, “the”, “and” and “to” are weak: /wi/, /kəd/, /tə/, /ðə/, /n/ and /tə/. They fit between the beats, so a long plan can be said at normal speed.
quests.phoneticRule: A multi-step plan has content words on the beats and a run of weak function words between them.
quests.spokenForm: Maybe wi kəd go tuh thuh cinema n then get something tuh eat

quests.instruction: Which links are heard in “Hi, I’m stuck, could you open it up for me?”
quests.word: Hi, I’m stuck, could you open it up for me
quests.textToSpeak: Hi, I’m stuck, could you open it up for me
options: Only “it up”; “open it” is separated
“open it” (the /n/ links) and “it up” (the /t/ links)
A linking /r/ in “up for”, and a glide in “open it”
Elision of the /n/ in “open”, and linking in “it up” as well
quests.correctAnswer: “open it” (the /n/ links) and “it up” (the /t/ links)
quests.hint: Check which words end in a consonant before a vowel-initial word.
quests.explanation: “Open” ends in /n/ before “it”, so the /n/ links. “It” ends in /t/ before “up”, so the /t/ links: “ope-ni-tup”. “Could you” also blends into /dʒ/. A polite request for help is full of small links, so listening for them helps you respond quickly.
quests.phoneticRule: A phrasal-verb request with “it” creates a chain of two consonant-to-vowel links.
quests.spokenForm: Hi, I’m stuck, cou-ja ope-ni-tup for me

quests.instruction: Which links are heard in “Listen, I’m lost, where is the nearest exit?”
quests.word: Listen, I’m lost, where is the nearest exit
quests.textToSpeak: Listen, I’m lost, where is the nearest exit
options: A linking /r/ in “nearest exit”, and elision in “where is”
An intrusive /r/ in “where is”, and a glide in “nearest exit” instead
No links, because the line is an urgent question
A linking /r/ in “where is”, and a linked /t/ in “nearest exit”
quests.correctAnswer: A linking /r/ in “where is”, and a linked /t/ in “nearest exit”
quests.hint: Find the word spelled with a final “r” and the word that ends in /t/ before a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Where” is spelled with a final “re”, so before the vowel of “is” a linking /r/ appears: “where-riz”. “Nearest” ends in /st/ before the vowel of “exit”, so the /t/ links: “neare-stexit”. A worried question still contains normal links. Hearing them helps you give the right answer.
quests.phoneticRule: Urgent questions use the same linking /r/ and consonant links as calm ones; urgency does not remove connected speech.
quests.spokenForm: Listen, I’m lost, where-riz the neare-stexit

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Oh dear, I’ve locked myself out of the house”?
quests.word: Oh dear, I’ve locked myself out of the house
quests.textToSpeak: Oh dear, I’ve locked myself out of the house
options: “myself out” is separated, and “out of” is fully pronounced as two strong words
“myself out” links the /f/ onto “out”, and “out of” links as “ou-təv”
A /tʃ/ blend in “locked myself”, and a glide in “out of”
Elision of the /f/ in “myself”, and assimilation in “out of”
quests.correctAnswer: “myself out” links the /f/ onto “out”, and “out of” links as “ou-təv”
quests.hint: Look for a consonant before a vowel in “myself out” and in “out of”.
quests.explanation: “Myself” ends in /f/ before the vowel of “out”, so the /f/ links: “myself-fout”. “Out” ends in /t/ before the weak “of”, so the /t/ links: “ou-təv”. A person locked out says this fast and urgently, so recognising the links helps you understand the problem.
quests.phoneticRule: A chain of fricative and plosive links appears in a short complaint, and “out of” is reduced to /aʊtəv/.
quests.spokenForm: Oh dear, I’ve locked myself-fout-təv the house

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “realise you” fits “Oh, I’m so sorry, I didn’t realise you were waiting”?
quests.word: Oh, I’m so sorry, I didn’t realise you were waiting
quests.textToSpeak: Oh, I’m so sorry, I didn’t realise you were waiting
options: “real-eye-zhoo”: the /z/ and /j/ blend into /ʒ/
“realise-you”: both sounds are separate
“real-eye-shoo”: they blend into /ʃ/
“real-eye-joo”: they blend into /dʒ/
quests.correctAnswer: “real-eye-zhoo”: the /z/ and /j/ blend into /ʒ/
quests.hint: Remember that “realise” ends in a /z/ sound, and keep the voicing in the blend.
quests.explanation: “Realise” ends in /z/ (spelled “se”), and “you” begins with /j/, so the pair blends into /ʒ/: “real-eye-zhoo”. An apology is spoken quickly, so the blend is very likely. Hearing it helps you follow the explanation.
quests.phoneticRule: A verb ending in /z/ blends with “you” into /ʒ/, even when the spelling uses “s” or “se”.
quests.spokenForm: Oh, I’m so sorry, I didn’t real-eye-zhoo were waiting

quests.instruction: What happens where “called” and “you” meet in “Apologies, I called you twice and left a message”?
quests.word: Apologies, I called you twice and left a message
quests.textToSpeak: Apologies, I called you twice and left a message
options: The /d/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
The /d/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/: “caal-joo”
The /l/ and /d/ are omitted before “you”
The two sounds stay separate, with a clear /j/
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/: “caal-joo”
quests.hint: The past-tense ending is a /d/ in “called”. Predict what a /d/ becomes before /j/.
quests.explanation: “Called” ends in the past-tense /d/, and “you” begins with /j/, so the pair blends into /dʒ/: “caal-joo”. The /l/ stays. Messages and explanations in apologies often contain such past-tense endings, which is why the blend appears so often.
quests.phoneticRule: Past-tense /d/ endings after /l/ still blend with a following “you” into /dʒ/.
quests.spokenForm: Apologies, I caal-joo twice and left a message

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “need you” fits “Tomorrow works for me, but I need you to confirm the time”?
quests.word: Tomorrow works for me, but I need you to confirm the time
quests.textToSpeak: Tomorrow works for me, but I need you to confirm the time
options: “need-you”: both words strong with a clear /j/
“nee-jew”: the /d/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/
“nee-chew”: they blend into /tʃ/
“nee-you”: the /d/ is omitted
quests.correctAnswer: “nee-jew”: the /d/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/
quests.hint: Say “need you” quickly and listen to what happens to the /d/.
quests.explanation: “Need” ends in /d/ and “you” begins with /j/, so the pair blends into /dʒ/: “nee-jew”. “To” is also weak: /tə/. Making an arrangement involves many sentences with “need you to”, so recognising the blend helps you understand what is being asked.
quests.phoneticRule: A main-verb /d/ before a weak “you” blends into /dʒ/, and the following “to” is typically weak.
quests.spokenForm: Tomorrow works for me, but I nee-jew tuh confirm the time

quests.instruction: Which words are weak in “Afternoon, I’m calling about the leak in the kitchen”?
quests.word: Afternoon, I’m calling about the leak in the kitchen
quests.textToSpeak: Afternoon, I’m calling about the leak in the kitchen
options: “calling”, “leak” and “kitchen”: the content words
Only “in” and “the”
None: phone calls need full forms
“I’m”, “about”, “the”, “in” and “the”
quests.correctAnswer: “I’m”, “about”, “the”, “in” and “the”
quests.hint: Pick out the problem words (calling, leak, kitchen) and treat the rest as quiet.
quests.explanation: The stressed words are “calling”, “leak” and “kitchen”. The small words “I’m”, “about”, “the”, “in” and “the” are weak, so the line sounds like “calling a-bout thuh leak in thuh kitchen”. A clear statement of the problem relies on stress, not full forms.
quests.phoneticRule: A phone report of a fault keeps stress on the problem words and reduces the function words.
quests.spokenForm: Afternoon, I’m calling about thuh leak in thuh kitchen

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Technically, it started on Monday and it’s getting worse”?
quests.word: Technically, it started on Monday and it’s getting worse
quests.textToSpeak: Technically, it started on Monday and it’s getting worse
options: “on” and “and” are strong, and the words are separated by clear breaks
“on” is weak, but “and” keeps /ænd/
“started on” blends into /dʒ/
“on” and “and” are weak, and “started on” links the /d/ onto “on”
quests.correctAnswer: “on” and “and” are weak, and “started on” links the /d/ onto “on”
quests.hint: Look for the small words and for the consonant before “on”.
quests.explanation: “Started” ends in /d/ before the vowel of “on”, so the /d/ links: “star-tidon”. “On” and “and” are function words and are weak. The stressed words are “started”, “Monday” and “worse”. A caller explaining a problem uses this rhythm.
quests.phoneticRule: A fault description combines linking with weak “on” and “and”, with stress on the time and the change.
quests.spokenForm: Technically, it star-tidon Monday n it’s getting worse

quests.instruction: Which reductions are heard in “Tomorrow morning is fine, as long as someone can let them in”?
quests.word: Tomorrow morning is fine, as long as someone can let them in
quests.textToSpeak: Tomorrow morning is fine, as long as someone can let them in
options: Strong “as” and “can”, and a clear /ð/ in “them” with no link before “in”
Weak “as” only; “can” and “them” are strong
Weak “as” and “can”, and a weak “them” that takes the /t/ of “let”
A /tʃ/ blend in “let them”, and strong “as”
quests.correctAnswer: Weak “as” and “can”, and a weak “them” that takes the /t/ of “let”
quests.hint: Check the three small words and the boundary before “in”.
quests.explanation: “As” is weak (/əz/), “can” is weak (/kən/), and “them” is weak (/əm/), with the /t/ of “let” linking onto it: “le-təm in”. The stressed words are “tomorrow”, “fine”, “long”, “let” and “in”. Arranging access with a landlord is full of these patterns.
quests.phoneticRule: A conditional arrangement combines weak “as”, weak “can” and a weak “them” that takes the preceding /t/ by linking.
quests.spokenForm: Tomorrow morning is fine, əz long əz someone kən le-təm in

quests.instruction: Which statements are true about “Cheers, I’d love to come, but I’ve got to work tomorrow”?
quests.word: Cheers, I’d love to come, but I’ve got to work tomorrow
quests.textToSpeak: Cheers, I’d love to come, but I’ve got to work tomorrow
options: “I’d” stands for “I would”, and “got to” may be said as “gotta”
“I’d” stands for “I had”, and “got to” may be said as “gonna”, because “gonna” means “got to”
“I’d” stands for “I did”, and “I’ve” is two full words
“I’d” stands for “I would”, but “got to” cannot be reduced
quests.correctAnswer: “I’d” stands for “I would”, and “got to” may be said as “gotta”
quests.hint: Look at the verb after “’d”, and recall the informal form of “got to”.
quests.explanation: “I’d love” has a base verb after “’d”, so it means “I would”. “I’ve got to” is often said as “I’ve gotta”. “Gonna” is for “going to”, not “got to”. The two contractions and the informal reduction combine in a polite decline.
quests.phoneticRule: A base verb after contracted /d/ signals “would”, and “got to” is reduced to “gotta”, not “gonna”.
quests.spokenForm: Cheers, I’d love tuh come, but I’ve gotta work tomorrow

quests.instruction: What do the contractions stand for in “Gran says she’s been waiting for ages, so we’d better hurry”?
quests.word: Gran says she’s been waiting for ages, so we’d better hurry
quests.textToSpeak: Gran says she’s been waiting for ages, so we’d better hurry
options: “she’s” stands for “she is”, and “we’d” for “we would”
“she’s” stands for “she was”, and “we’d” for “we did”
“she’s” stands for “she has”, and “we’d” for “we would”, as in “we would better”
“she’s” = “she has” (before “been”), and “we’d” = “we had” (in “we’d better”)
quests.correctAnswer: “she’s” = “she has” (before “been”), and “we’d” = “we had” (in “we’d better”)
quests.hint: Look at the form of the verb after each contraction.
quests.explanation: “She’s been” needs the auxiliary “has”, because “been” is a past participle. “We’d better” is the fixed expression “we had better”. The same sounds /z/ and /d/ can therefore stand for different words, and only grammar tells you which.
quests.phoneticRule: Contracted ’s is “has” before a past participle, and contracted ’d in “’d better” is “had”.
quests.spokenForm: Gran says sheez been waiting for ages, so weed better hurry

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Auntie says they’re going to be late, so don’t wait for them”?
quests.word: Auntie says they’re going to be late, so don’t wait for them
quests.textToSpeak: Auntie says they’re going to be late, so don’t wait for them
options: “they’re gonna be late, so doan’ wait fuh ’em”: contraction, “gonna”, weak /t/ and weak “for them”
“they are going to be late, so do not wait for them”, all words strong
“they’re gonta be late, so don-tuh wait for them”
“their gonna be late, so doan’ wait for them”: “their” in place of “they’re”, which sound alike but are spelled differently
quests.correctAnswer: “they’re gonna be late, so doan’ wait fuh ’em”: contraction, “gonna”, weak /t/ and weak “for them”
quests.hint: Combine the contraction, the informal form, the negative and the weak words.
quests.explanation: “They’re” is a contraction, “going to” becomes “gonna”, “don’t” has a weak /t/ before “wait”, and “for them” is weak: /fə rəm/. The sentence is easy to say but hard to hear if you expect full forms. Each reduction is independent, so you can recognise them one at a time.
quests.phoneticRule: A final social line can combine a standard contraction, an informal reduction, a negative contraction and weak function words.
quests.spokenForm: Auntie says they’re gonna be late, so doan’ wait fuh ’em
